newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Vietnam leads Asia invective against U.S. attacks.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam leads Asia invective against U.S. attacks.

text.p: Vietnam led the Asian charge on Wednesday against U.S. attacks on Iraq by denouncing its former enemy while China accused President Bill Clinton of flexing American military muscle in the Gulf to get re-elected.

Australia said Washington was tough but right, Taiwan gave its wholehearted support and Japan, the world's biggest importer of Middle East oil, called for a quick resolution to the most serious U.S.-Iraqi confrontation since the Gulf War.

As a second wave of U.S. cruise missiles was fired at southern Iraq targets in retaliation for Iraqi military strikes on the country's Kurdish north, Vietnam said it was following the situation "with deep concern".

"Regardless of the circumstance, to use force against a sovereign state is contrary to international law, is not in line with the common global trend, and is unacceptable," a Vietnamese Foreign Ministry spokesman said in a statement.
Vietnam, which fought the Americans in a drawn-out and bloody war that ended 21 years ago, was also critical of the U.S.-led military campaign against Iraq in the Gulf War.

China's official Xinhua news agency said "the strike served... Clinton's need to strengthen his image and influence as a world political leader at home so as to win the upcoming presidential elections in November".

The strike was a ploy to expand U.S. military presence in the Gulf to reinforce its control of the oil-rich region, Xinhua said in a commentary, quoting what it described as an "Oriental military expert" whom it did not identify.
"The U.S. desperately needed to make a good show in containing the Iraqis to offset its impotence in bolstering the stalled peace process" in the Middle East, Xinhua said.
On Wednesday, China's Foreign Ministry spokesman expressed deep regret and grave concern over the missile attacks and renewed tension in the Gulf.
Indonesia expressed concern about "territorial integrity" and urged restraint by both sides.
"In this context, Indonesia reiterates its basic stand that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Iraq should be respected," Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi, reading a statement after a cabinet meeting, called on the United States to refrain from further attacks on Iraq and urged Baghdad to stop military action against its Kurdish minority.

It described the U.S. attacks as "harsh, punitive action, undertaken without first exhausting all other available avenues" and urged Iraq "to refrain from engaging in further military action in the Kurdish areas which might provoke an aggravation of the situation".
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer called the second U.S. cruise missile attack tough but right.

"It is tough action but it is tough action which we think is understandable and we support it," Downer told reporters. "Let us hope that (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein understands the mistake he has made and that he begins to behave in a responsible way. It is in everybody's interest that he does."
Japan, a strong backer of U.S. action against Iraq, called for Baghdad to withdraw immediately its forces from Kurdish areas of the country.
In comments earlier on Wednesday before the second U.S. attack, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was concerned at the size of the forces Iraq was moving into Kurdish areas.
Taiwan was brief in its reaction but to the point.
"The Foreign Ministry thinks the U.S. government's action is justified and appropriate," it said in a statement.
